title: NRI Deposits Hit Record $127 Billion as RBI Closes FCNR Scheme Ahead of Schedule
excerpt: India's diaspora-focused dollar deposit scheme attracted nearly five times the amount raised in the 2013 iteration, pushing forex reserves toward $750 billion and prompting the RBI to close the window a month early.
body:
• India's FCNR(B) deposit scheme attracted $127.23 billion in NRI deposits by the August 31 deadline — nearly five times the $26 billion raised when the scheme was last used in 2013.
  • Total forex inflows under the RBI's swap facility reached $136.38 billion, including external commercial borrowings and overseas foreign currency borrowings.
  • The RBI closed the deposit window a month early on August 31, ahead of the original September 30 deadline, citing overwhelming response.
  • India's forex reserves hit a record $729.33 billion and are projected to cross $750 billion by September-end.

India's bet on its diaspora to shore up the rupee has paid off at a scale that even the Reserve Bank of India did not anticipate. NRI deposits under the Foreign Currency Non-Resident (FCNR(B)) scheme reached $127.23 billion by August 31, the RBI confirmed on Wednesday — a figure so large that the central bank shut the deposit window a full month ahead of the original September 30 deadline.

The total foreign currency inflows under the RBI's concessional swap facility stood at $136.38 billion as of August 31, with the lion's share coming through diaspora deposits. Banks also raised $3.89 billion through external commercial borrowings and $5.26 billion through overseas foreign currency borrowings.

From $26 Billion to $127 Billion

The numbers represent a dramatic escalation from any previous effort to tap the Indian diaspora for foreign currency support. When the FCNR(B) scheme was last deployed in 2013 during a rupee crisis, it attracted approximately $26 billion. The current mobilization is nearly five times that figure.

The RBI introduced the scheme in June 2026 as part of a package of measures to stabilize the rupee, which had fallen to record lows earlier this year amid rising oil prices and global dollar strength. Banks were permitted to offer higher interest rates on FCNR deposits for a limited period, and could swap the dollars with the RBI for rupees at zero cost — giving them access to cheaper rupee funding while simultaneously boosting the central bank's reserves.

"This is clearly larger than expectations. This should give comfort to the RBI on currency, and their ability to manage volatility. Also, it helps understand why they closed the FCNR(B) window earlier than initial schedule."

— Vivek Rajpal, Asia Strategist, JB Drax Honore (UK)

Reserves Head Toward $750 Billion

India's foreign exchange reserves were already at an all-time high of $729.33 billion in the week ended August 21, before the final surge of deposits in the closing days of August. Gaura Sen Gupta, chief economist at IDFC FIRST Bank, estimates reserves are likely to cross $750 billion by the end of September as more of these inflows are swapped with the RBI.

The massive inflows have given the central bank significantly more firepower to defend the rupee. The RBI has already stepped up dollar sales in recent days to support the currency, traders told Reuters. However, the sheer volume of dollar liquidity entering the system creates its own challenges.

"With a record quantum of durable U.S. dollar liquidity entering the system in a relatively compressed time frame, it would be compelling for the RBI to sterilise the resultant rupee liquidity," said Siddharth Kothari, economist at Sunidhi Securities, suggesting the central bank may need to raise the Cash Reserve Ratio to absorb excess liquidity.

What It Means for NRIs

The record mobilization underscores the financial weight of India's 32-million-strong diaspora. For NRIs who deposited funds, the scheme offered an attractive combination: higher-than-market interest rates on dollar deposits parked in Indian banks, with the added safety of sovereign-backed institutional accounts. The deposits are denominated in foreign currency, meaning NRIs bear no exchange rate risk.

However, former RBI Governor D. Subbarao cautioned that FCNR deposits are "borrowed dollars" that must eventually be repaid. "They do not build confidence," he told Bloomberg. "What we need is confidence-building flows through foreign direct and portfolio investment."

The scheme's closure also means NRIs who missed the August 31 deadline can no longer access the concessional rates, though the window for bank borrowings through external commercial borrowings and overseas foreign currency borrowings remains open.

Rupee Outlook

Analysts expect the rupee to remain broadly stable in the near term, supported by the massive reserves buffer. IDFC FIRST Bank projects the currency at around 96 per dollar by December, while Karur Vysya Bank expects a range of 94.5 to 96.5 through 2026. The trajectory will depend increasingly on crude oil prices, global dollar conditions, and the RBI's willingness to keep intervening in the market.
